title: Answer to Question: The Reality of the International Position towards North Korea's Nuclear Tests
text:
Answer to Question: The reality of the international position towards North Korea's nuclear tests

Question:

On 25/5/2009 North Korea announced that it had conducted a successful nuclear test. It had earlier threatened, on the 8th of this month (May), to strengthen its nuclear force, and accused the Obama administration of continuing hostile acts against it. It has refused to return to the Six-Party talks. On 27/5/2009 it announced that it is "not bound by the armistice signed between it and America, in response to South Korea's participation in the American security initiative to prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons" (Al Jazeera, 31/5/2009).

So what is the reality of the international position towards these events? Are matters moving towards escalation to the brink of a war..., or is war unlikely, and matters will return to negotiations?

Answer:

Yes, matters have become hotter, especially after North Korea's announcement that it is not bound by the armistice, which is the armistice that was signed between North Korea and America on 27/7/1953, under which the Korean War that broke out on 25/6/1950 stopped, without a peace agreement being signed between them. The heat had become noticeable since North Korea conducted its first nuclear test in October 2006, then it became hotter when last month it conducted a test of a ballistic missile, which means that it is able to launch its nuclear bomb with a long-range missile and not carry it by an aircraft that can be intercepted and prevented from reaching its target. And it became hotter still a few days ago, on 25/5/2009 CE, when North Korea announced that it had conducted another successful nuclear test.

As for the international position:

1- Worldwide reactions were issued calling for a resolution to be obtained in the UN Security Council to punish it, whereupon Korea threatened to undertake other steps. The official North Korean news agency on 25/5/2009 quoted a spokesman of the North Korean Foreign Ministry as saying: "If the Security Council undertakes new provocations, we will have no choice but to take additional steps to defend ourselves."

2- As for the reaction of the United States of America, its President Barack Obama stated: "North Korea's nuclear and missile programmes pose a grave threat to peace and security in the world. I strongly condemn this reckless action of hers. North Korea's actions threaten the people of North-East Asia, and they also constitute a blatant violation of international law and contradict commitments that North Korea had previously given. Now the United States and the international community must take measures in response to this" (Russia Today, 25/5/2009). And the US Defence Secretary Robert Gates stated at the security and defence conference held in Singapore that "the United States will not accept the existence of a nuclear-armed North Korea. And he warned of the outbreak of a nuclear arms race." And he said: "The United States will not stand idly by while North Korea continues its capability to wreak havoc on any target it wants." And he said: "The administration of Barack Obama will hold Pyongyang fully responsible for the transfer of nuclear technology, whether to states or to non-official organisations, considering it a grave threat to the United States and its allies" (Al Jazeera, 30/5/2009). Thus by these statements America has shown its displeasure at North Korea's conduct, and indicated that it threatens world peace, and particularly the region of North-East Asia. And it, that is America, will take measures against North Korea, and America has warned it against transferring nuclear technology to other states or non-official organisations.

America's story with North Korea's nuclear programme did not begin yesterday; rather it began in 1986, when America requested information and details about its nuclear programme and Korea refused to hand them over to it, and handed them to China, the number of documents being 19 thousand pages. An agreement was reached between America and North Korea in 1994 CE, after America threatened to strike North Korea's nuclear reactor. This agreement stipulated that North Korea would stop its nuclear programme and close its nuclear reactor at Yongbyon, in which it had begun its nuclear activity in 1987, in return for America providing it with two nuclear reactors working with light water. But America did not fulfil its promises, so Korea resumed its nuclear activity, restarted the Yongbyon reactor and expelled the international monitors from the country at the end of 2002, following America's accusation of North Korea that it had a secret nuclear programme, and North Korea's accusation of America of backing out of its promises to provide two nuclear reactors working with light water. In October 2006 North Korea announced the conducting of its first nuclear test. In February 2007 agreement was reached in the Six-Party talks, which include North Korea itself, America, Russia, China, Japan and South Korea, on closing its Yongbyon nuclear reactor in return for aid given to it to supply it with fuel. America announced that it would give North Korea 25 million dollars. After these funds were transferred to North Korea, the inspection teams and monitors were permitted to enter and the Yongbyon reactor was closed. In July 2008 North Korea handed over its report on its nuclear programme within the framework of the deal of its abandoning its nuclear programme. Their talks stopped at the end of last year, 2008, following disagreements between them because of the call to verify North Korea's compliance with the commitments it had undertaken in the previous agreements. At the beginning of this year it announced its withdrawal from the Six-Party talks and the restarting of its nuclear reactor at Yongbyon, after it expelled the international inspectors from the country and threatened to resume its nuclear tests. And last month, at the beginning of April, it conducted a test launch of a long-range missile carrying a satellite, as it stated. The Security Council took a resolution condemning it and requesting the application of the sanctions against it that had previously been frozen, after Security Council resolution number 1718 in 2006, following its conducting of its first nuclear test. So it announced a second time, on 14/4/2009, following the Security Council resolution issued one day before that date, that it had withdrawn from the Six-Party talks, and announced that there was no use in them and that it was not bound by any agreements concluded during the Six-Party talks. And several days ago, that is on the 25th of this month (May), it announced the successful conducting of its second test.

It is clear from that that America was working to deceive North Korea so that it would stop all its nuclear activity in return for nothing except false promises and commitments, or commitments whose fulfilment it delays or from which, or from part of which, it retreats. However, North Korea was aware, so whenever it saw evasion from America it returned to resuming its nuclear activity. It appears that America is not decisive to the very end in this matter. Perhaps what prevents it from that is that it does not want to strain its relations with China and create a rupture between them, because it has interests in China more important and greater than the North Korean nuclear reactor.

It is also understood from America's actions and statements, and the reactions to them in that region, that it has other aims, among them strengthening its presence in the region so as to keep its control over it tight, such that the states of the region remain in need of American protection, so that it can blackmail and exploit them, especially as it has a large military presence in this region, where the number of American forces is about 250 thousand American soldiers. So we see the US Defence Secretary Robert Gates holding a special meeting with the defence ministers of South Korea and Japan on the sidelines of the security conference currently being held in Singapore, and announcing after this meeting: "It is important that South Korea, Japan, the United States and the whole world cooperate so that multiple parties confront this problem" (Radio Sawa, 31/5/2009). This means that America is trying to exploit this problem to extend its hegemony over the region and to prove its leadership of the world, and to frighten China that it, that is America, might ignite a war there with its neighbour and ally North Korea at any moment. That is, through this problem America is trying to blackmail China into extracting concessions from it, and facilities in the economy, trade and finance and in policy related to the region, and to prevent the annexation of Taiwan to China or delay it, and to remain encircling China and stationed on its borders on the pretext of North Korea and its nuclear weapons and missiles. This is not strange for America, for it markets the installation of anti-missiles in Poland and radars in the Czech Republic directed towards Russia on the pretext of the Korean missiles, and then the Iranian ones.

3- As for the position of China: following North Korea's latest nuclear test, China's position was calling for calm and resort to diplomacy. The chief of the Chinese General Staff, Lieutenant General Ma Xiaotian, called at the security and defence conference held in Singapore for "following a method of calm and deliberation regarding North Korea, and called for the region to be cleared of weapons of mass destruction" (Al Jazeera, 30/5/2009), which indicates that China does not accept the striking of North Korea. China also exploits this issue, as America has also exploited it. It, that is China, uses the card of its support for North Korea in its issue of the island of Taiwan, in order to annex it to itself, trying to use it as a pressure card against America so that America accepts China's annexation of the island of Taiwan. So China, as is America, is trying to exploit the problem with regard to Taiwan, but in two opposite directions.

4- As for South Korea, it does not want matters to become more tense and for a war to happen at its expense. The South Korean Defence Minister Lee Sang-hee stated at this conference: "His country will work to solve the crisis with North Korea within the framework of the Six-Party talks and the international community" (the same previous source). South Korea had been working continuously for reconciliation with North Korea, and two summits were held between their two presidents in 2000 and in 2007, all of that at the initiative of South Korea.

5- As for the position of Russia, the media office of the Russian President announced, following telephone talks between the Russian President Medvedev and the Prime Minister of Japan Taro Aso, that "the two sides agreed on the necessity of taking the strongest reaction towards these actions, which represent a challenge to the international security system" (Russia Today, 30/5/2009). Alexander Borodavkin, the Russian Deputy Foreign Minister, had earlier called on Pyongyang to refrain from launching its ballistic missile (Russia Today, 27/3/2009). This indicates that Russia's position on North Korea differs from the Chinese position, and that Russia aims at good relations with Japan by taking this position. It has no interest in North Korea developing its nuclear and missile programmes, and it does not want America to take it as a means to tighten its control in the region. It wants it to remain in the whirlpool of talks within the framework of the Six-Party talks and not leave them until a solution is reached that stops it from developing its nuclear and missile programmes, and consequently ends what is called the question of the Korean peninsula.

6- As for the heat of the events leading to the outbreak of a war, in other words America launching a war on Korea's nuclear installations, this is unlikely, at least in the foreseeable term. America did not undertake the like of this when North Korea did not possess the nuclear bomb and did not possess ballistic missiles, at a time when America knew that Korea was moving towards that and expected it to reach nuclear capability. So how then would it launch a war on it now, when it has come to possess nuclear weapons, especially as Korea's relationship with China is still strong? That is why the possibility of America launching a war now on North Korea, after it has come to possess this capability, this possibility is weak and unlikely, as we said, at least in the foreseeable term. But what is expected is that America will resort to other means in an attempt to contain North Korea, by way of negotiations and enticements, and by way of South Korea drawing close to it by various means so that it can penetrate it, and create channels of contact with some helpers inside, and then a change of the leadership in it, and the coming of more moderate leaderships, that is, the coming of a leadership that can come to an understanding with America and accept its offers or enticements, as happened in all the socialist states that had adopted Communism, especially as North Korea suffers from a pressing economic crisis and a suffocating isolation... And all of that, even if its results are not guaranteed, it is expected that America will exert every effort in it.
